prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of large room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance and its realisation in magnetic tunnel junctions, enabling spintronic read heads and magnetic memory

statement.case_for: I keep tunnel magnetoresistance first. The 1995 room-temperature results of Miyazaki and Moodera made spin-dependent tunnelling a robust, reproducible effect, and Parkin's work on coherent MgO junctions and their industrial development carried it from a laboratory curiosity into read heads and MRAM. What I value most is that the physics is closed: the large TMR in MgO has a transparent electronic-structure origin, symmetry-selective Delta-1 tunnelling, which first-principles calculations predicted and experiment then confirmed. Three decades of replication and universal adoption mean the field has had every chance to settle, so the recognition is overdue rather than early. It is also a distinct mechanism from the giant magnetoresistance honoured in 2007, so I do not regard it as double-counting. Nobody else ranked B037 in the openings, and I do not take that as a verdict on its merit. It sits in a corner of magnetism that colleagues in AMO, particle and astroparticle physics may not have weighed closely.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is attribution. The 2004 coherent-tunnelling MgO step is also credited to Yuasa and Djayaprawira, who are not in the credited names, so the trio covers the discovery and industrial optimisation better than every link of the MgO story. There is also a reasonable argument that the 2007 GMR prize already covers the spin-electronics territory and that the committee will not want a second award there. Finally, I am the only member to place it first, so I must be careful not to promote it on a subfield affinity that colleagues do not share.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first: the magic-wavelength idea removes the trapping light shift, clocks reach about 1e-18, and a clean two-person Katori and Ye prize is possible, although Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde have claims on the Sr lattice clock.
responses.response: I moved up on B042 after reading this. I had ranked it fifth, mainly worried about overlap with the 2005 comb prize. Kroll and Lindroth argue convincingly that the lattice idea is a distinct invention, and the 10^-18 comparisons across several laboratories are very strong evidence. I still disagree with Kroll on one point. Calling the Katori and Ye pairing clean understates the problem that Ido, Takamoto and Lemonde are outside it, and the committee should settle whether the prize is for the concept or the record accuracy. That is the same kind of credit problem I accept in my own preferred case, so it does not separate the two. It makes B042 my first alternative, and it is a serious rival to B037.

responses.point: Olsson puts B042 first and also B007 third, arguing that the clock case is mature, well-timed with the possible redefinition of the second, and that the topological insulators case is mature but must be weighed against the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I agree with her on the maturity of B007 and share the 2016 concern. We both ranked it high, and I would be comfortable with it as an alternative. My reservation is that Kane and Mele, with Molenkamp, leave out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp realised. Calling this a complete account of the HgTe observation is therefore too generous. I would not call the three names wrong, but the citation would need careful wording so that it does not claim more than the trio delivered. For that reason I rank TMR first, where the credited names cover the discovery and development with fewer holes.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the ATLAS and CMS Higgs observation first on the grounds that it is decisive and long confirmed, while accepting that credit in collaborations of thousands is hard to allocate and that spokespersons could be argued.
responses.response: I agree the discovery is scientifically decisive; I placed it sixth only because of attribution. My disagreement is that Danielsson treats the founding-leader trio as natural. The prize cannot go to collaborations, and the founding proposers did not make the 2012 observation. Spokespersons at the time of discovery or analysis leaders have an equally credible claim, and none of those options is obviously correct. I would not block B026 on scientific grounds, but I think its attribution problem is greater than that of a three-person experimental and industrial achievement such as TMR.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality class first and magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene third, noting that the superconducting mechanism is still unsettled and argues for some patience.
responses.response: On B054 I agree with his patience point more than my opening ranking suggested. I ranked it second for the unusually tight link between the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model and the 2018 experiment. The pairing mechanism is still debated, and the leading experimentalist, Cao, is not credited, so I now treat it as promising but early and have not made it a preferred or alternative case. I cannot say much on KPZ, which lies outside my expertise and which B034 stays outside my configuration for that reason. His point that Parisi's 1986 co-authorship complicates the attribution is one I would have to take seriously.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the MgO coherent-tunnelling credit as covered when Yuasa and Djayaprawira are outside the trio.
Whether TMR is judged sufficiently distinct from the 2007 giant magnetoresistance prize.
Whether the lattice-clock priority among Katori, Ye, Ido, Takamoto and Lemonde can be settled well enough for B042 to be the better choice.
How much weight a single first-place ranking from one member should carry when no colleague has yet argued against or for it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. B037 lies close to my field of theoretical magnetism, but I have no documented connection to Moodera, Parkin or Miyazaki. My co-authors and collaborators in the profile are not among the credited names.
